title: SVM & Kernels
summary: Maximum-margin classification and the kernel trick — a classic algorithm that still gets asked in interviews long after it left most production stacks.

slides.markdown:
A **support vector machine** doesn't just find *a* line that separates two classes — it finds the one that stays **as far as possible** from both classes, the widest possible margin.

That single idea, plus a trick for handling non-linear boundaries without ever leaving linear-algebra land, made SVMs the state of the art before deep learning. They're less common in production now, but interviewers still love them for how cleanly they test geometric intuition.

Infinitely many lines can separate two linearly-separable classes. An SVM picks the one that maximizes the **margin** — the distance from the boundary to the nearest point of either class.

The intuition for why that's the right choice: a boundary that barely squeezes between the classes is fragile — a slightly different test point flips its prediction. A boundary with maximum breathing room on both sides generalizes better, because small perturbations in new data are less likely to cross it.

slides.subTitle: Support vectors and the margin
slides.markdown:
Only the points closest to the boundary — the **support vectors** — actually determine where it sits; every other point could move or vanish without changing the fit.

![Support vectors defining the maximum-margin boundary between two classes](assets/svm-margin.svg)

That's a distinctive property: unlike linear regression, where every point pulls on the fit, an SVM's solution depends only on the handful of points sitting right at the edge.

assets.alt: Support vectors defining the maximum-margin boundary between two classes

slides.subTitle: The C parameter
slides.markdown:
Real data is rarely perfectly separable, so SVMs allow some points to sit on the wrong side of the margin (or the boundary itself) via a **soft margin**, controlled by the parameter `C`.

- **Large `C`** — heavily penalize violations → narrower margin, fits training data closely, more prone to overfitting.
- **Small `C`** — tolerate more violations → wider margin, smoother boundary, more bias but often better generalization.

`C` is the same bias-variance dial you see everywhere else, just wearing a different name.

Many datasets aren't linearly separable in their original feature space, but *are* separable if you map them into a higher-dimensional space first. Computing that mapping explicitly is often expensive or even infinite-dimensional.

The **kernel trick** sidesteps this: SVM training only ever needs the **dot product** between pairs of transformed points, and a kernel function computes that dot product directly from the original features — without ever materializing the high-dimensional vectors. You get the benefit of a non-linear mapping at the computational cost of a linear one.

slides.subTitle: Common kernels
slides.markdown:
Three kernels cover most real use:

- **Linear** — no transformation; use when classes are already roughly linearly separable, or with very high-dimensional sparse data (text).
- **RBF (Gaussian)** — the default general-purpose choice; implicitly maps to infinite dimensions, flexible enough for most non-linear boundaries.
- **Polynomial** — captures interactions up to a chosen degree; less common in practice, more sensitive to tuning.

Start with linear on high-dimensional data, RBF otherwise — then tune from there.

Both draw linear boundaries by default, but optimize for different things.

| | SVM | Logistic regression |
|---|---|---|
| Optimizes | Maximum margin | Log-likelihood |
| Output | Class label (margin) | Calibrated probability |
| Non-linear boundary | Kernel trick | Manual feature engineering |
| Sensitivity | Only to support vectors | To all points |

Pick SVM with a kernel for a hard non-linear boundary on modest data; pick logistic regression when you need real probabilities or must scale to huge datasets.

**The mistake:** reaching for a kernel SVM on millions of rows, expecting it to train like a linear model.

**Why it breaks:** kernel SVM training scales roughly quadratically to cubically with sample count, since it computes pairwise kernel values across the training set. Past a few hundred thousand rows, training time turns impractical — the core reason SVMs faded from large-scale production.

**The fix:** at real scale, prefer a linear model or tree ensemble; reserve kernel SVMs for smaller, harder-boundary problems.
